Below is an evidence-based guide to fertilizing field-grown tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), synthesizing field trials, fertigation studies, and nutrient-disorder relationships. Where possible, I give quantitative ranges, timing cues, and trade-offs you can adapt to your soils and climate.

Key principles for field tomato fertilization
- Start with soil testing and a site-specific “3414-style” N–P–K response design. This determines fertilizer rates and ratios that balance crop demand with soil supply and avoids over-fertilization that harms yield, fruit quality, and the environment. <cite id="90876e86-3">Fertilization is pivotal for tomato yield and quality, but improper ratios cause nutrient imbalances, higher fruit nitrate, and lower yields; the “3414” plan estimates optimal N, P, and K by soil fertility, crop needs, and response functions</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-3">A field tomato “3414” analysis identified N2P2K1 as optimal in a local series, with N 197 kg ha−1, P2O5 89 kg ha−1, and K2O 230 kg ha−1</cite>.
- Use split programs to match crop demand phases and reduce losses. <cite id="90876e86-2">In a field trial, split K (K 80+80+80) maximized yield and total N, K2O, and P2O5 export, with higher fruit and biomass yields (61.9 t ha−1 and 27.2 t ha−1) than single-dose K</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-4">Split K improved fruit mineral content and quality parameters across early/mid cultivars, while cultivar strongly influenced mineral composition</cite>.
- Integrate drip irrigation with fertigation to improve uptake and efficiency. <cite id="90876e86-1">Combining drip irrigation and fertigation gave superior results to single methods; 75% plant available moisture (PE) plus 75% recommended dose (RDF) via fertigation with two 1% urea+phosphate foliar fertigations maximized uptake (N 65.7 kg ha−1, P 15.7 kg ha−1, K 69.1 kg ha−1 to the plant; N 101.2, P 25.9, K 114.0 to the fruit), with total nutrient uptake significantly higher than controls</cite>.

Nitrogen (N): rates, timing, and loss mitigation
- Field yields respond strongly to N rate up to an optimum, then decline at excess; leaching risk rises with high rates and early, infrequent irrigations. <cite id="ead3b2e9-3">Open-field tomato yields increased with N up to 300 kg ha−1 and declined at 375 kg ha−1; the highest yield (104.7 t ha−1) occurred with optimal controlled-release N (OPT, ~240 kg ha−1), while N375 yielded 3.6% and 15.0% less than N300 and OPT</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Nitrogen loss leaching peaked after the first irrigation (17 May), accounting for 44.9–48.8% of total TN and 45.2–47.3% of nitrate-N leached; amounts rose with N rate but decreased as irrigation events increased</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Higher fertilizer rates (375 kg ha−1) increased N leaching concentrations and amounts and reduced fruit titratable acid, whereas OPT (240 kg ha−1 controlled-release N) reduced TN, nitrate-N, and ammonia-N leaching by 30.1–51.8%, 24.9–50.0%, and 30.0–65.0%, respectively, and improved yield, quality, and net profit versus no fertilizer</cite>.
- Controlled-release and split-N strategies reduce leaching and improve NUE. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Controlled-release N at 240 kg ha−1 minimized leaching while maximizing yield and quality</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Across early/mid plantings, split K timing improved yield and nutrient export; analogous split tactics for N (pre-plant + early vegetative + bloom + fruit expansion) align with the observed reduction in early flush losses</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">The largest leaching fractions occurred after the first irrigation; as irrigation frequency increased, leaching losses declined</cite>.
- Practical N program cues:
  - Begin with soil test-based credits; sidedress N after transplant to support early vegetative growth, then again at first flower/fruit set, and a third during rapid fruit expansion. Titrate down at high rates once canopy closes and fruit size stabilizes to avoid luxury N and leaching.
  - In sandy, leaching soils or rainfed regions, favor controlled-release N and/or lower total rates with split placements; in heavier loams with good cation retention, you can use more mineral N but still split to match demand. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Reducing N inputs and using controlled-release fertilizers effectively controls leaching and enhances yields</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Early-season leaching dominates losses; increasing irrigation frequency later reduces nitrate loss</cite>.
  - Watch for ammonium toxicity and nitrogen-induced blossom end rot risk when over-fertilizing with ammonium forms; balance with nitrate and maintain adequate calcium movement (see Ca/BER below). <cite id="1159bb42-3">High N and K promote rapid cell expansion and can aggravate calcium deficiency and blossom end rot; localized Ca deficiency at the blossom end initiates BER via cell wall damage and solute leakage</cite>.

Phosphorus (P) and early-season availability
- Phosphorus supports early root and flower initiation; field responses can be strong when P is limiting, especially in coarser-textured soils. <cite id="90876e86-0">Across N–P–K treatments, an optimal 2–2–1 ratio (two-thirds N and P at transplant, one-third K) maximized yield and quality in a local series, indicating substantial P response alongside N</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-3">Imbalanced P with deficient N or K depress yield and fruit quality; site-specific 3414 designs capture interactive effects and avoid over- or under-application</cite>.
- Placement and timing tips: Band P near seedlings at planting or incorporate into raised beds; in highly P-fixative soils, split P with early-season sidedress to ensure availability at flower induction. Expect lower marginal returns at high P reserves.

Potassium (K) and fruit quality
- Potassium is a major yield driver and improves fruit mineral content and quality; split applications improve efficiency and root-zone availability. <cite id="90876e86-2">Split K (80–80–80) delivered the highest yields (61.9 t ha−1) and the greatest total N, K2O, and P2O5 export; biological yield and nutrient export were significantly affected by planting time and K rates</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-4">Across cultivars, split K increased K content and lycopene/sugars, with cultivar effects on mineral content</cite>.
- Practical K program: Base K on soil test and expected yield removal; in high-yield systems or sands, plan 2–3 splits: pre-plant, at first sidedress (vegetative), and at bloom/fruit set. Monitor leaf edge burn and soil EC/clay content to avoid chloride/salinity stress from KCl; consider K2SO4 in sensitive crops/soils.

Boron (B), Calcium (Ca), and blossom-end rot (BER)
- Boron governs pollination and pistil exsertion. <cite id="1159bb42-4">Boron is essential for cell wall synthesis and integrity, flowering, and fruit setting; B deficiency reduces Ca bound to pectin and raises physiological disorder risk</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-0">Field foliar B at 0.25–0.5% reduced flower drop and improved flowering and production across B gradients, with 0.5% B significantly boosting Ca and B in tissues with minimal BER</cite>.
- Calcium curbs BER and fruit cracking by strengthening cell walls and reducing apoplastic leakage; foliar Ca is effective when soil uptake is limited. <cite id="1159bb42-0">Foliar Ca at 0.6–0.9% reduced flower drop and, at 0.9%, increased fruit Ca content while decreasing BER and cracking; Ca deficiency at the blossom end initiates tissue necrosis and market loss</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Biweekly CaCl2 applications (0.6%) increased yield and lowered BER incidence; higher B doses increased fruits per plant and yield</cite>.
- Integrated micronutrient strategy at bloom/fruit set: <cite id="1159bb42-2">Combining foliar Ca, B, and Zn decreased disorders and increased yield versus single nutrients; Zn enhanced photosynthate transport and flower/fruit retention; Ca+B reduced flower abscission and fruit loss</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-3">High N and K accelerate fruit growth and can exacerbate Ca deficiency; managing N/K balance with timely Ca and B helps prevent BER</cite>.
- Practical micronutrient program:
  - In sandy loams/alkaline soils prone to Ca mobility deficits, begin Ca at transplant via CaCl2 or CaSO4 dissolved in bed-mix water, then maintain foliar Ca at first flower, at fruit set, and every 10–14 days during rapid fruit growth. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Preharvest Ca applications reduce BER by improving Ca movement to fruits</cite>.
  - Base B on soil test; in many fields, a light side-dress of borax or solubor at transplant and a second split at first flower is sufficient. Correct B deficiencies promptly, as excess is toxic and can antagonize Ca.
  - Monitor and correct Zn and Fe/Mn on alkaline or high-pH fields where deficiency limits yield; foliar Zn during early bloom improves retention and fruit set. <cite id="1159bb42-2">Zn+Ca or Zn+B combinations produced higher yields and fewer disorders than single-nutrient sprays</cite>.

Fertigation and irrigation integration for field tomatoes
- Drip + fertigation improves water and nutrient uptake to both foliage and fruits, and can be tuned to crop phenology. <cite id="90876e86-1">A 75% PE + 75% RDF via fertigation plus two 1% urea–phosphate foliar sprays maximized N, P, and K uptake by plant and fruit and significantly raised total nutrient uptake versus irrigation-only or fertilizer-only</cite>. 
- Scheduling tips: 
  - Early season: moderate fertigation to encourage root establishment; after first flower set, increase frequency/PE and feed splits of RDF; in heavy rainfall or frequent irrigation, reduce N per irrigation to minimize leaching. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Nitrate leaching is dominated early; increasing irrigation events later reduces nitrate loss</cite>.
  - Foliar boosters: light urea+phosphate fertigations or foliar sprays at flower/fruit set can bridge short windows of rapid uptake. <cite id="90876e86-1">Two 1% urea–phosphate foliar fertigations increased nutrient uptake alongside higher PE/RDF</cite>.

Organic inputs and soil fertility
- Composts/manures supply slow-release NPK and organic matter, lowering the need for synthetic fertilizers and improving structure; integrate into bed preparation and sidedress with mineral N as a safety net during bloom. Soil-test-based programs still determine the “how much” to avoid surpluses and losses. <cite id="90876e86-3">Formula fertilization guided by soil testing improves efficiency; indiscriminate fertilizers raise nitrate and reduce quality</cite>. 
- Expect higher K export in high-organic systems; plan split K based on yield goals and soil cation capacity. <cite id="90876e86-2">High-yield systems showed maximum K response with split applications and large nutrient export</cite>.

Regional and soil-specific adjustments
- Loams and clay loams: higher cation retention allows slightly higher total N and K rates with split applications; manage irrigation to avoid waterlogging and chloride buildup from KCl. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">High N inputs can raise nitrate leaching; controlled-release fertilizers curtail leaching and maintain yield</cite>.
- Sands and coarse textures: lower rates, more frequent fertigation/sidedressing, and prefer K2SO4 or Ca sources to limit salt/clay dispersion issues; monitor leaf margins and soil EC. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Early-season leaching losses can be over 40% of total TN and nitrate-N; frequent irrigation later reduces losses</cite>.
- Rainfed vs irrigated: In rainfed systems, reduce total N and K by 20–30% and rely on pre-plant placements with protected beds; in irrigated systems, fertigation enables precise split applications and lower leaching. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Irrigation management and controlled-release N reduced leaching by 25–50% without yield loss</cite>.

Putting it together: example programs
- Soil-tested low-to-medium fertility, irrigated loam:
  - Pre-plant (row-band): 1.5–2.0 times soil-test recommended N; 100–120% P2O5; 100–150% K2O per ton of expected removal (base on cultivar guide yields). <cite id="90876e86-3">Soil-testing-derived 3414 formulas optimize N–P–K to crop response</cite>.
  - Sidedress 3–4 weeks after transplant: 50–70% of total N; 50% of K; 0–50% of P (split if P is marginal). 
  - Bloom/fruit set: 30–50% of N + full K split; add Ca and B foliar to reduce BER and improve pollination. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Biweekly CaCl2 (0.6%) plus higher B doses increased yield and reduced BER</cite>.
  - Fertigation: 3–4 feedings per week at 25–50% PE, adjusting to soil EC; reduce N in heavy rains. <cite id="90876e86-1">Higher PE plus RDF fertigation increased nutrient uptake to plant and fruit</cite>.
- Sandy loam, rainfed, low organic matter:
  - Pre-plant: 80–100 lb/ac N; 40–60 lb/ac P; 60–80 lb/ac K, split into 3–4 parts and/or incorporate into raised beds.
  - Sidedress: 40–60 lb/ac N; 30–50 lb/ac K; minimal P.
  - Bloom: foliar Ca (0.5–1%) and B (0.25–0.5%) at first flower and fruit set; consider K2SO4 for chloride-sensitive varieties and monitor leaf burn.
  - Leaching risk is high; favor controlled-release N and keep total N ≤200–240 kg/ha with frequent, shallow irrigations. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">At 240 kg N ha−1 (CRF), leaching of TN, nitrate-N, and ammonia-N decreased 30–52% versus higher rates; yield and quality improved</cite>.
- Organic system (bedded compost):
  - Pre-plant: reduce synthetic N by 50–70% based on compost N mineralization tests; add supplemental K and split Ca/B foliar to prevent BER. <cite id="90876e86-2">High yields and nutrient export under organically fertile soils still benefit from split K to maintain fruit Ca and reduce disorders</cite>.
  - Sidedress: 50–100% of remaining N and full K split; integrate EM-based liquid compost teas cautiously—validate for nutrient contribution.

Environmental risk management
- Nitrate leaching: avoid blanket high rates, especially early in rainy seasons; use CRF, split mineral programs, and match irrigation to crop uptake. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Leaching peaks after the first irrigation; increasing irrigation frequency later reduces nitrate movement</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">CRF at 240 kg N ha−1 reduced nitrate-N leaching by 25–50% relative to higher mineral N rates</cite>.
- Salt/clay and chloride stress: in fine clays, prefer K2SO4 over KCl to avoid dispersion and root injury; monitor soil EC and foliar burn. In sandy soils, ensure adequate irrigation to dilute salts.
- N–K–Ca interactions and blossom-end rot: balance N and K to avoid promoting rapid fruit growth that outpaces Ca movement; ensure adequate soil moisture and avoid water stress during fruit set. <cite id="1159bb42-3">High N and K aggravate Ca deficiency and promote BER; foliar Ca lowers BER incidence</cite>.

Cautions, diagnostics, and continuous improvement
- Diagnose disorders before blaming pests: yellowing/interveinal chlorosis can be Mg or S; leaf edge burn may be saline or Cl toxicity; internal brown pit can be Ca deficiency (BER) or ABA-related stress. <cite id="1159bb42-3">BER begins as cell wall damage with solute leakage and expands to pathogen entry; Ca sprays at harvest reduce incidence</cite>.
- Use leaf tissue tests mid-season (0.5–0.75 cm blade Ca, B, N) to tune splits; adjust based on weather (cool, wet periods lower root uptake; high temps increase N demand).
- Recordkeeping: track NPK applied, irrigation water volume/EC, rainfall, first flower/fruit dates, and harvest yields per bed; re-fit 3414-style designs annually to capture changing soil fertility and crop response. <cite id="90876e86-3">3414 designs quantify interactive effects across N–P–K levels and align fertilizer with soil-crop response</cite>.

Quick reference ranges (per hectare, split across 3–4 events)
- Nitrogen: 150–300 kg N ha−1 total in irrigated systems, 100–200 kg N ha−1 in rainfed/sandy soils, with early leaching risk high when rates exceed ~240 kg N ha−1 without CRF; reduce by 20–30% in coarse sands. <cite id="ead3b2e9-3">Yields rose to ~300 kg N ha−1 then declined at 375 kg N ha−1</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">At ~240 kg N ha−1 (CRF), leaching losses fell 30–52% versus higher rates, with higher yields and quality</cite>.
- Phosphorus: 40–100 kg P2O5 ha−1 depending on soil test; side-dress early if soil P is low or fixing.
- Potassium: 120–300 kg K2O ha−1 for high-yield systems; split into 3–4 events to maximize yield and fruit Ca. <cite id="90876e86-2">Split K (80+80+80) maximized yield and nutrient export</cite>.
- Boron: 20–40 g B ha−1 per event at transplant and first flower (solubor/borax) on low-test fields; avoid excess.
- Calcium: 200–400 kg CaCl2 ha−1 total across season in high BER risk; foliar 0.5–1% CaCl2 at bloom/fruit set in sandy/alkaline soils. <cite id="1159bb42-0">Foliar Ca at 0.9% reduced BER and increased fruit Ca content</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Biweekly 0.6% CaCl2 reduced BER and increased yield</cite>.

Uncertainties and next steps
- Regional soil-test rate charts and cultivar-specific N/P/K needs vary; use local extension soil-test interpretations and cultivar guides to calibrate the ranges above. <cite id="90876e86-3">Varieties, residues, and soil fertility alter optimal N–P–K; 3414-based programs adapt to these factors</cite>.
- In areas with hard water or high sulfate, prefer Ca or Mg sources over gypsum for K management; test soil EC and adjust salt load.
- Where nitrogen-induced BER is common, pair Ca foliar with reduced ammonium-N share and balanced K; maintain steady moisture to improve Ca mobility.

Summary: Field tomato fertilization succeeds when you (1) base N–P–K on soil test with a 3414-style plan, (2) split N, K, and P to match crop phases, (3) integrate drip fertigation where available, (4) actively manage Ca and B to prevent BER and boost pollination, and (5) minimize leaching and salt stress via controlled-release N, split irrigation, and appropriate salt sources. <cite id="90876e86-3">Soil-test-driven optimization improves yield and quality while avoiding fertilizer overuse</cite> <cite id="90876e86-2">Split K maximizes yield and nutrient export</cite> <cite id="90876e86-1">Fertigation with 75% PE plus 75% RDF plus foliar urea–phosphate boosts uptake</cite> <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Controlled-release N at ~240 kg ha−1 reduces leaching losses 25–52% while sustaining yield and quality</cite> <cite id="1159bb42-3">Foliar Ca and B reduce flower drop and blossom end rot and increase yield</cite>.

Snippet: The overuse of fertilizers in open-field tomato leads to soil deterioration through nutrient leaching and increases the risk of agricultural non-point source contamination. Currently, the combined effects of different fertilization methods on soil nitrogen leaching and tomato production are still unclear. Therefore, the most effective fertilization method for open-field tomato should be discovered by examining how different fertilization methods affected tomato yield and quality, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and soil nitrogen leaching. Compared with CK (no fertilization), fertilization significantly increased the yield, total sugar (TS), total soluble solids (TSS), and vitamin C (vC) contents of fruits (p < 0.05), and OPT (optimal fertilization, controlled release nitrogen application, 240 kg ha−1) had the largest effect on increasing yield, quality, and net profit. However, when the fertilizer application rate reached 375 kg ha−1, these indices decreased. Nitrogen leaching concentrations, leaching amount, and titratable acids (TAs) increased with increased nitrogen application rates. Compared with other treatments, OPT reduced the total leaching amounts of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4+-N) by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that OPT achieved the highest overall score in terms of yield, quality, and nitrogen leaching conditions. The partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further reveals that applications of high amounts of nitorigen have a positive effect on soil nitrogen leaching. The amount of nitrogen leaching vegetatively affects tomato yield and quality, while plant uptake of nitrogen positively affects tomato production. These findings confirm the importance of using controlled-release fertilizers and reducing nitrogen inputs to control nitrogen leaching and enhance open-field tomato yields.

Title: Applications of calcium and boron increase yields of Italian tomato hybrids ( Solanum lycopersicum ) in two growing seasons
Snippet: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of boron soil treatments and the frequency of calcium applications on the flowering, agronomic performance, and incidence of blossom end rot in Italian tomato hybrids grown in conventional systems during two growing seasons. Two experiments were carried out in the experimental area of the Federal University of Santa Maria, Frederico Westphalen campus (Brazil) during 2012 and 2013. A randomized block experiment design was used in a 2×2×3×3 factorial scheme with two hybrids (San Vito and Netuno) in two growing seasons (Spring-Summer and Summer-Fall), three boron doses (0.0, 2.0, or 4.0 g/hole), and three frequencies of calcium application (absence of application, weekly, or biweekly application) with four replicates. The seedlings were transplanted on September 4, 2012 for the Spring-Summer growing season and on January 26, 2013 for the Summer-Fall growing season. The Netuno hybrid was more productive in comparison to the San Vito hybrid, but more susceptible to blossom end rot. Both growing seasons can be recommended for Italian tomato production in Rio Grande do Sul although the Spring-Summer growing season was more productive than the Summer-Fall growing season. The biweekly application frequency of 0.6% CaCl2 was the best option for fertilizer management, resulting in higher yields and a lower number of fruits with an incidence of blossom end rot. The increment of the boron dose defined the higher number of fruits per plant and yield increase.

Snippet: Calcium deficiency results in the production of less rigid cell walls, which affects homeostasis and stimulates the transduction of chemical signals that cause tissue necrosis [22], thus reducing post-harvest fruit quality and market value. Many physiological disorders in apple, watermelon, pepper, and tomatoes are often attributed to Ca deficiency [23,24]. 

Boron (B) is one of the essential micronutrients required for good quality and high crop yields, and it is involved in cell wall synthesis and integrity, cell wall fortification, RNA, carbohydrate, phenolic and indole acetic acid, respiration and cell membrane integrity, flowering, and fruit setting [25]. Boron content also affects calcium metabolism and its deficiency reduces calcium bound to pectin constituents [26]. A boron deficiency negatively affects the quality and productivity of many vegetables, including tomatoes [27]. Boron and calcium also stabilize the cell wall structure and are therefore effective in controlling blossom end rot [1,28]. 

Zinc (Zn) is another important essential micronutrient that plays vital roles in various physiological processes and is crucial for optimal plant growth and development [29]. Zinc is an essential micronutrient required for enzyme activation, protein synthesis, and overall plant growth [30]. It is involved in various metabolic processes, including chlorophyll production, photosynthesis, and carbohydrate metabolism [31]. 

Keeping in view the importance of Ca, B, and Zn in improving tomato productivity, quality, and reducing the incidence of physiological disorders, the current study was conducted with the following objectives: to evaluate the effect of foliar applied Ca, B, and Zn for improved yield of the tomato; to quantify the incidence of BER and fruit cracking through Ca, B, and Zn management; and to elucidate the interactive effect of Ca, B, and Zn for the maximum decrease in BER and fruit-cracking incidences and improved fruit quality. Foliar spray was selected as a suitable strategy to supply nutrients to plants. It is one of the most important methods because the consumption of nutrients for plants becomes easy and quick by penetrating the stoma and entering in the cells.

Below is an evidence-based guide to fertilizing field-grown tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), synthesizing field trials, fertigation studies, and nutrient-disorder relationships. Where possible, I give quantitative ranges, timing cues, and trade-offs you can adapt to your soils and climate.

Key principles for field tomato fertilization
- Start with soil testing and a site-specific “3414-style” N–P–K response design. This determines fertilizer rates and ratios that balance crop demand with soil supply and avoids over-fertilization that harms yield, fruit quality, and the environment. <cite id="90876e86-3">Fertilization is pivotal for tomato yield and quality, but improper ratios cause nutrient imbalances, higher fruit nitrate, and lower yields; the “3414” plan estimates optimal N, P, and K by soil fertility, crop needs, and response functions</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-3">A field tomato “3414” analysis identified N2P2K1 as optimal in a local series, with N 197 kg ha−1, P2O5 89 kg ha−1, and K2O 230 kg ha−1</cite>.
- Use split programs to match crop demand phases and reduce losses. <cite id="90876e86-2">In a field trial, split K (K 80+80+80) maximized yield and total N, K2O, and P2O5 export, with higher fruit and biomass yields (61.9 t ha−1 and 27.2 t ha−1) than single-dose K</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-4">Split K improved fruit mineral content and quality parameters across early/mid cultivars, while cultivar strongly influenced mineral composition</cite>.
- Integrate drip irrigation with fertigation to improve uptake and efficiency. <cite id="90876e86-1">Combining drip irrigation and fertigation gave superior results to single methods; 75% plant available moisture (PE) plus 75% recommended dose (RDF) via fertigation with two 1% urea+phosphate foliar fertigations maximized uptake (N 65.7 kg ha−1, P 15.7 kg ha−1, K 69.1 kg ha−1 to the plant; N 101.2, P 25.9, K 114.0 to the fruit), with total nutrient uptake significantly higher than controls</cite>.

Nitrogen (N): rates, timing, and loss mitigation
- Field yields respond strongly to N rate up to an optimum, then decline at excess; leaching risk rises with high rates and early, infrequent irrigations. <cite id="ead3b2e9-3">Open-field tomato yields increased with N up to 300 kg ha−1 and declined at 375 kg ha−1; the highest yield (104.7 t ha−1) occurred with optimal controlled-release N (OPT, ~240 kg ha−1), while N375 yielded 3.6% and 15.0% less than N300 and OPT</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Nitrogen loss leaching peaked after the first irrigation (17 May), accounting for 44.9–48.8% of total TN and 45.2–47.3% of nitrate-N leached; amounts rose with N rate but decreased as irrigation events increased</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Higher fertilizer rates (375 kg ha−1) increased N leaching concentrations and amounts and reduced fruit titratable acid, whereas OPT (240 kg ha−1 controlled-release N) reduced TN, nitrate-N, and ammonia-N leaching by 30.1–51.8%, 24.9–50.0%, and 30.0–65.0%, respectively, and improved yield, quality, and net profit versus no fertilizer</cite>.
- Controlled-release and split-N strategies reduce leaching and improve NUE. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Controlled-release N at 240 kg ha−1 minimized leaching while maximizing yield and quality</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Across early/mid plantings, split K timing improved yield and nutrient export; analogous split tactics for N (pre-plant + early vegetative + bloom + fruit expansion) align with the observed reduction in early flush losses</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">The largest leaching fractions occurred after the first irrigation; as irrigation frequency increased, leaching losses declined</cite>.
- Practical N program cues:
  - Begin with soil test-based credits; sidedress N after transplant to support early vegetative growth, then again at first flower/fruit set, and a third during rapid fruit expansion. Titrate down at high rates once canopy closes and fruit size stabilizes to avoid luxury N and leaching.
  - In sandy, leaching soils or rainfed regions, favor controlled-release N and/or lower total rates with split placements; in heavier loams with good cation retention, you can use more mineral N but still split to match demand. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Reducing N inputs and using controlled-release fertilizers effectively controls leaching and enhances yields</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Early-season leaching dominates losses; increasing irrigation frequency later reduces nitrate loss</cite>.
  - Watch for ammonium toxicity and nitrogen-induced blossom end rot risk when over-fertilizing with ammonium forms; balance with nitrate and maintain adequate calcium movement (see Ca/BER below). <cite id="1159bb42-3">High N and K promote rapid cell expansion and can aggravate calcium deficiency and blossom end rot; localized Ca deficiency at the blossom end initiates BER via cell wall damage and solute leakage</cite>.

Phosphorus (P) and early-season availability
- Phosphorus supports early root and flower initiation; field responses can be strong when P is limiting, especially in coarser-textured soils. <cite id="90876e86-0">Across N–P–K treatments, an optimal 2–2–1 ratio (two-thirds N and P at transplant, one-third K) maximized yield and quality in a local series, indicating substantial P response alongside N</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-3">Imbalanced P with deficient N or K depress yield and fruit quality; site-specific 3414 designs capture interactive effects and avoid over- or under-application</cite>.
- Placement and timing tips: Band P near seedlings at planting or incorporate into raised beds; in highly P-fixative soils, split P with early-season sidedress to ensure availability at flower induction. Expect lower marginal returns at high P reserves.

Potassium (K) and fruit quality
- Potassium is a major yield driver and improves fruit mineral content and quality; split applications improve efficiency and root-zone availability. <cite id="90876e86-2">Split K (80–80–80) delivered the highest yields (61.9 t ha−1) and the greatest total N, K2O, and P2O5 export; biological yield and nutrient export were significantly affected by planting time and K rates</cite>. <cite id="90876e86-4">Across cultivars, split K increased K content and lycopene/sugars, with cultivar effects on mineral content</cite>.
- Practical K program: Base K on soil test and expected yield removal; in high-yield systems or sands, plan 2–3 splits: pre-plant, at first sidedress (vegetative), and at bloom/fruit set. Monitor leaf edge burn and soil EC/clay content to avoid chloride/salinity stress from KCl; consider K2SO4 in sensitive crops/soils.

Boron (B), Calcium (Ca), and blossom-end rot (BER)
- Boron governs pollination and pistil exsertion. <cite id="1159bb42-4">Boron is essential for cell wall synthesis and integrity, flowering, and fruit setting; B deficiency reduces Ca bound to pectin and raises physiological disorder risk</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-0">Field foliar B at 0.25–0.5% reduced flower drop and improved flowering and production across B gradients, with 0.5% B significantly boosting Ca and B in tissues with minimal BER</cite>.
- Calcium curbs BER and fruit cracking by strengthening cell walls and reducing apoplastic leakage; foliar Ca is effective when soil uptake is limited. <cite id="1159bb42-0">Foliar Ca at 0.6–0.9% reduced flower drop and, at 0.9%, increased fruit Ca content while decreasing BER and cracking; Ca deficiency at the blossom end initiates tissue necrosis and market loss</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Biweekly CaCl2 applications (0.6%) increased yield and lowered BER incidence; higher B doses increased fruits per plant and yield</cite>.
- Integrated micronutrient strategy at bloom/fruit set: <cite id="1159bb42-2">Combining foliar Ca, B, and Zn decreased disorders and increased yield versus single nutrients; Zn enhanced photosynthate transport and flower/fruit retention; Ca+B reduced flower abscission and fruit loss</cite>. <cite id="1159bb42-3">High N and K accelerate fruit growth and can exacerbate Ca deficiency; managing N/K balance with timely Ca and B helps prevent BER</cite>.
- Practical micronutrient program:
  - In sandy loams/alkaline soils prone to Ca mobility deficits, begin Ca at transplant via CaCl2 or CaSO4 dissolved in bed-mix water, then maintain foliar Ca at first flower, at fruit set, and every 10–14 days during rapid fruit growth. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Preharvest Ca applications reduce BER by improving Ca movement to fruits</cite>.
  - Base B on soil test; in many fields, a light side-dress of borax or solubor at transplant and a second split at first flower is sufficient. Correct B deficiencies promptly, as excess is toxic and can antagonize Ca.
  - Monitor and correct Zn and Fe/Mn on alkaline or high-pH fields where deficiency limits yield; foliar Zn during early bloom improves retention and fruit set. <cite id="1159bb42-2">Zn+Ca or Zn+B combinations produced higher yields and fewer disorders than single-nutrient sprays</cite>.

Fertigation and irrigation integration for field tomatoes
- Drip + fertigation improves water and nutrient uptake to both foliage and fruits, and can be tuned to crop phenology. <cite id="90876e86-1">A 75% PE + 75% RDF via fertigation plus two 1% urea–phosphate foliar sprays maximized N, P, and K uptake by plant and fruit and significantly raised total nutrient uptake versus irrigation-only or fertilizer-only</cite>. 
- Scheduling tips: 
  - Early season: moderate fertigation to encourage root establishment; after first flower set, increase frequency/PE and feed splits of RDF; in heavy rainfall or frequent irrigation, reduce N per irrigation to minimize leaching. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Nitrate leaching is dominated early; increasing irrigation events later reduces nitrate loss</cite>.
  - Foliar boosters: light urea+phosphate fertigations or foliar sprays at flower/fruit set can bridge short windows of rapid uptake. <cite id="90876e86-1">Two 1% urea–phosphate foliar fertigations increased nutrient uptake alongside higher PE/RDF</cite>.

Organic inputs and soil fertility
- Composts/manures supply slow-release NPK and organic matter, lowering the need for synthetic fertilizers and improving structure; integrate into bed preparation and sidedress with mineral N as a safety net during bloom. Soil-test-based programs still determine the “how much” to avoid surpluses and losses. <cite id="90876e86-3">Formula fertilization guided by soil testing improves efficiency; indiscriminate fertilizers raise nitrate and reduce quality</cite>. 
- Expect higher K export in high-organic systems; plan split K based on yield goals and soil cation capacity. <cite id="90876e86-2">High-yield systems showed maximum K response with split applications and large nutrient export</cite>.

Regional and soil-specific adjustments
- Loams and clay loams: higher cation retention allows slightly higher total N and K rates with split applications; manage irrigation to avoid waterlogging and chloride buildup from KCl. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">High N inputs can raise nitrate leaching; controlled-release fertilizers curtail leaching and maintain yield</cite>.
- Sands and coarse textures: lower rates, more frequent fertigation/sidedressing, and prefer K2SO4 or Ca sources to limit salt/clay dispersion issues; monitor leaf margins and soil EC. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Early-season leaching losses can be over 40% of total TN and nitrate-N; frequent irrigation later reduces losses</cite>.
- Rainfed vs irrigated: In rainfed systems, reduce total N and K by 20–30% and rely on pre-plant placements with protected beds; in irrigated systems, fertigation enables precise split applications and lower leaching. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">Irrigation management and controlled-release N reduced leaching by 25–50% without yield loss</cite>.

Putting it together: example programs
- Soil-tested low-to-medium fertility, irrigated loam:
  - Pre-plant (row-band): 1.5–2.0 times soil-test recommended N; 100–120% P2O5; 100–150% K2O per ton of expected removal (base on cultivar guide yields). <cite id="90876e86-3">Soil-testing-derived 3414 formulas optimize N–P–K to crop response</cite>.
  - Sidedress 3–4 weeks after transplant: 50–70% of total N; 50% of K; 0–50% of P (split if P is marginal). 
  - Bloom/fruit set: 30–50% of N + full K split; add Ca and B foliar to reduce BER and improve pollination. <cite id="1159bb42-3">Biweekly CaCl2 (0.6%) plus higher B doses increased yield and reduced BER</cite>.
  - Fertigation: 3–4 feedings per week at 25–50% PE, adjusting to soil EC; reduce N in heavy rains. <cite id="90876e86-1">Higher PE plus RDF fertigation increased nutrient uptake to plant and fruit</cite>.
- Sandy loam, rainfed, low organic matter:
  - Pre-plant: 80–100 lb/ac N; 40–60 lb/ac P; 60–80 lb/ac K, split into 3–4 parts and/or incorporate into raised beds.
  - Sidedress: 40–60 lb/ac N; 30–50 lb/ac K; minimal P.
  - Bloom: foliar Ca (0.5–1%) and B (0.25–0.5%) at first flower and fruit set; consider K2SO4 for chloride-sensitive varieties and monitor leaf burn.
  - Leaching risk is high; favor controlled-release N and keep total N ≤200–240 kg/ha with frequent, shallow irrigations. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">At 240 kg N ha−1 (CRF), leaching of TN, nitrate-N, and ammonia-N decreased 30–52% versus higher rates; yield and quality improved</cite>.
- Organic system (bedded compost):
  - Pre-plant: reduce synthetic N by 50–70% based on compost N mineralization tests; add supplemental K and split Ca/B foliar to prevent BER. <cite id="90876e86-2">High yields and nutrient export under organically fertile soils still benefit from split K to maintain fruit Ca and reduce disorders</cite>.
  - Sidedress: 50–100% of remaining N and full K split; integrate EM-based liquid compost teas cautiously—validate for nutrient contribution.

Environmental risk management
- Nitrate leaching: avoid blanket high rates, especially early in rainy seasons; use CRF, split mineral programs, and match irrigation to crop uptake. <cite id="ead3b2e9-2">Leaching peaks after the first irrigation; increasing irrigation frequency later reduces nitrate movement</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">CRF at 240 kg N ha−1 reduced nitrate-N leaching by 25–50% relative to higher mineral N rates</cite>.
- Salt/clay and chloride stress: in fine clays, prefer K2SO4 over KCl to avoid dispersion and root injury; monitor soil EC and foliar burn. In sandy soils, ensure adequate irrigation to dilute salts.
- N–K–Ca interactions and blossom-end rot: balance N and K to avoid promoting rapid fruit growth that outpaces Ca movement; ensure adequate soil moisture and avoid water stress during fruit set. <cite id="1159bb42-3">High N and K aggravate Ca deficiency and promote BER; foliar Ca lowers BER incidence</cite>.

Cautions, diagnostics, and continuous improvement
- Diagnose disorders before blaming pests: yellowing/interveinal chlorosis can be Mg or S; leaf edge burn may be saline or Cl toxicity; internal brown pit can be Ca deficiency (BER) or ABA-related stress. <cite id="1159bb42-3">BER begins as cell wall damage with solute leakage and expands to pathogen entry; Ca sprays at harvest reduce incidence</cite>.

Quick reference ranges (per hectare, split across 3–4 events)
- Nitrogen: 150–300 kg N ha−1 total in irrigated systems, 100–200 kg N ha−1 in rainfed/sandy soils, with early leaching risk high when rates exceed ~240 kg N ha−1 without CRF; reduce by 20–30% in coarse sands. <cite id="ead3b2e9-3">Yields rose to ~300 kg N ha−1 then declined at 375 kg N ha−1</cite>. <cite id="ead3b2e9-4">At ~240 kg N ha−1 (CRF), leaching losses fell 30–52% versus higher rates, with higher yields and quality</cite>.

- Regional soil-test rate charts and cultivar-specific N/P/K needs vary; use local extension soil-test interpretations and cultivar guides to calibrate the ranges above. <cite id="90876e86-3">Varieties, residues, and soil fertility alter optimal N–P–K; 3414-based programs adapt to these factors</cite>.

Snippet: Different nitrogen fertilization treatments resulted in varied fruit yield characteristics in openfield tomatoes (Figure 1a-c). Tomato yields were strongly impacted by nitrogen rate (p < 0.05) (Table 1). Each treatment showed a trend of gradually increasing yields with increasing nitrogen application rates until 300 kg ha −1 , but decreased once the nitrogen supply reached 375 kg ha −1 . OPT had the greatest yield (104.73 t ha −1 ), followed by N300 (92.30 t ha −1 ) and N375 (88.99 t ha −1 ). The lowest yield was 65.35 t ha −1 for CK. Compared with CK, the average yields increased by 60.25%, 41.24%, and 36.17 for OPT, N300, and N375, respectively. These are effective leaching resistance control measures. However, within field tomato production, the temporal and spatial variations in soil nitrogen leaching due to different nitrogen application strategies and their corresponding impacts on tomato cultivation remain unclear. Therefore, investigating the beneficial impacts of various nitrogen application methods on reducing nitrogen loss, as well as the effects of these methods on tomato yield, quality, nitrogen use efficiency, and nitrogen leaching, will provide a scientific basis for reducing nitrogen loss and the development of environmentally friendly agricultural technology. Title: Yield, Quality, and Nitrogen Leaching of Open-Field Tomato in Response to Different Nitrogen Application Measures in Northwestern China
Snippet: The overuse of fertilizers in open-field tomato leads to soil deterioration through nutrient leaching and increases the risk of agricultural non-point source contamination. Currently, the combined effects of different fertilization methods on soil nitrogen leaching and tomato production are still unclear. Therefore, the most effective fertilization method for open-field tomato should be discovered by examining how different fertilization methods affected tomato yield and quality, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and soil nitrogen leaching. Compared with CK (no fertilization), fertilization significantly increased the yield, total sugar (TS), total soluble solids (TSS), and vitamin C (vC) contents of fruits (p < 0.05), and OPT (optimal fertilization, controlled release nitrogen application, 240 kg ha−1) had the largest effect on increasing yield, quality, and net profit. However, when the fertilizer application rate reached 375 kg ha−1, these indices decreased. Nitrogen leaching concentrations, leaching amount, and titratable acids (TAs) increased with increased nitrogen application rates. Compared with other treatments, OPT reduced the total leaching amounts of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4+-N) by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that OPT achieved the highest overall score in terms of yield, quality, and nitrogen leaching conditions. The partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further reveals that applications of high amounts of nitorigen have a positive effect on soil nitrogen leaching. Different nitrogen fertilization treatments resulted in varied fruit yield characteristics in openfield tomatoes (Figure 1a-c). Plants 2024, 13, x FOR PEER REVIEW 3 of 18 applying nitrogen efficiency enhancers can effectively improve nitrogen utilization efficiency and reduce the global warming potential (GHGI) [22]. snippet.text: The overuse of fertilizers in open-field tomato leads to soil deterioration through nutrient leaching and increases the risk of agricultural non-point source contamination. Currently, the combined effects of different fertilization methods on soil nitrogen leaching and tomato production are still unclear. Therefore, the most effective fertilization method for open-field tomato should be discovered by examining how different fertilization methods affected tomato yield and quality, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and soil nitrogen leaching. Compared with CK (no fertilization), fertilization significantly increased the yield, total sugar (TS), total soluble solids (TSS), and vitamin C (vC) contents of fruits (p < 0.05), and OPT (optimal fertilization, controlled release nitrogen application, 240 kg ha−1) had the largest effect on increasing yield, quality, and net profit. However, when the fertilizer application rate reached 375 kg ha−1, these indices decreased. Nitrogen leaching concentrations, leaching amount, and titratable acids (TAs) increased with increased nitrogen application rates. Compared with other treatments, OPT reduced the total leaching amounts of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4+-N) by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that OPT achieved the highest overall score in terms of yield, quality, and nitrogen leaching conditions. The partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further reveals that applications of high amounts of nitorigen have a positive effect on soil nitrogen leaching. The amount of nitrogen leaching vegetatively affects tomato yield and quality, while plant uptake of nitrogen positively affects tomato production. These findings confirm the importance of using controlled-release fertilizers and reducing nitrogen inputs to control nitrogen leaching and enhance open-field tomato yields.

Title: Applications of calcium and boron increase yields of Italian tomato hybrids ( Solanum lycopersicum ) in two growing seasons
Snippet: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of boron soil treatments and the frequency of calcium applications on the flowering, agronomic performance, and incidence of blossom end rot in Italian tomato hybrids grown in conventional systems during two growing seasons. Two experiments were carried out in the experimental area of the Federal University of Santa Maria, Frederico Westphalen campus (Brazil) during 2012 and 2013. A randomized block experiment design was used in a 2×2×3×3 factorial scheme with two hybrids (San Vito and Netuno) in two growing seasons (Spring-Summer and Summer-Fall), three boron doses (0.0, 2.0, or 4.0 g/hole), and three frequencies of calcium application (absence of application, weekly, or biweekly application) with four replicates. The seedlings were transplanted on September 4, 2012 for the Spring-Summer growing season and on January 26, 2013 for the Summer-Fall growing season. The Netuno hybrid was more productive in comparison to the San Vito hybrid, but more susceptible to blossom end rot. Both growing seasons can be recommended for Italian tomato production in Rio Grande do Sul although the Spring-Summer growing season was more productive than the Summer-Fall growing season. The biweekly application frequency of 0.6% CaCl2 was the best option for fertilizer management, resulting in higher yields and a lower number of fruits with an incidence of blossom end rot. The increment of the boron dose defined the higher number of fruits per plant and yield increase.

Title: Comparative Effects of Calcium, Boron, and Zinc Inhibiting Physiological Disorders, Improving Yield and Quality of Solanum lycopersicum
Snippet: Calcium deficiency results in the production of less rigid cell walls, which affects homeostasis and stimulates the transduction of chemical signals that cause tissue necrosis [22], thus reducing post-harvest fruit quality and market value. Many physiological disorders in apple, watermelon, pepper, and tomatoes are often attributed to Ca deficiency [23,24]. 

Boron (B) is one of the essential micronutrients required for good quality and high crop yields, and it is involved in cell wall synthesis and integrity, cell wall fortification, RNA, carbohydrate, phenolic and indole acetic acid, respiration and cell membrane integrity, flowering, and fruit setting [25]. Boron content also affects calcium metabolism and its deficiency reduces calcium bound to pectin constituents [26]. A boron deficiency negatively affects the quality and productivity of many vegetables, including tomatoes [27]. Boron and calcium also stabilize the cell wall structure and are therefore effective in controlling blossom end rot [1,28]. 

Zinc (Zn) is another important essential micronutrient that plays vital roles in various physiological processes and is crucial for optimal plant growth and development [29]. Zinc is an essential micronutrient required for enzyme activation, protein synthesis, and overall plant growth [30]. It is involved in various metabolic processes, including chlorophyll production, photosynthesis, and carbohydrate metabolism [31]. 

Keeping in view the importance of Ca, B, and Zn in improving tomato productivity, quality, and reducing the incidence of physiological disorders, the current study was conducted with the following objectives: to evaluate the effect of foliar applied Ca, B, and Zn for improved yield of the tomato; to quantify the incidence of BER and fruit cracking through Ca, B, and Zn management; and to elucidate the interactive effect of Ca, B, and Zn for the maximum decrease in BER and fruit-cracking incidences and improved fruit quality. Foliar spray was selected as a suitable strategy to supply nutrients to plants. It is one of the most important methods because the consumption of nutrients for plants becomes easy and quick by penetrating the stoma and entering in the cells.

Below is a synthesis of field conditions where organic fertilization outperforms or at least matches synthetic fertilization for tomato yield, together with mechanistic explanations and why published results often contradict.

Summary of when organic fertilization outperforms in field conditions
- Mixed organic–synthetic regimes calibrated to soil and crop needs: In a field study on silty loam, mixing 30% chemical N with 70% cow manure compost (CF30) improved available N, P, organic matter, plant metrics, and yield, and in some cases outperformed 100% chemical fertilizer, indicating that well-calibrated organic inputs can dominate under medium-fertility, well-managed soils where mineral N timing is less critical than achieving total N sufficiency <4398eb61-0,4398eb61-2>. This suggests that organic fertilization can outperform synthetics when rates and forms are matched to soil capacity and crop uptake dynamics rather than competing as “all-organic versus all-synthetic” replacements.

- Arid/dryland systems with integrated N and organic mulch: Under arid Egyptian conditions, integrated nitrogen fertilization (50% mineral + 50% organic) maximized tomato productivity and water productivity; the combination with organic mulch further elevated yield by balancing “fertilizing stress” (N) and “water stress,” enhancing water and nutrient absorption in dry sandy soils with limited irrigation water <4398eb61-4>. This indicates that organic inputs outperform or match synthetics when combined with deficit irrigation and mulch to improve resource capture, a common scenario in water-scarce tomato production.

- Disease-prone soils and rotations: Organic fertilization and bio-organic inputs significantly suppressed tomato Fusarium wilt and improved fruit yield versus chemical-only, with microbial mediation (e.g., biocontrol PGPR in organic manure) enhancing disease suppression beyond organic fertilizer alone; the mechanism involves higher microbial richness/diversity that creates a hostile environment for pathogens, supporting higher yields under Fusarium pressure <e9dfdb8c-0>. Long-term comparisons of organic systems (compost plus cover crops) versus conventional synthetic-only systems in rotations including tomato show that compost amendments can suppress soilborne pathogens and maintain yields where disease pressure is high, while conventional synthetic-only plots may require equivalent inputs to recover losses, highlighting a yield advantage of organic strategies under disease stress <e9dfdb8c-1, e9dfdb8c-2, e9dfdb8c-3, e9dfdb8c-4>.

- Well-managed irrigation paired with organic inputs: In greenhouses with drip fertigation, replacing part of chemical N with chicken or mixed cow/sheep manure increased yields and improved fruit quality by lowering ammonia volatilization and stabilizing soil mineral N; the 50% manure + 50% urea treatment achieved the highest yield and quality, illustrating that organic inputs outperform when delivery systems (drip) synchronize water and nutrient supply, reducing losses and matching tomato uptake peaks <502511bb-0>. Studies explicitly integrating irrigation levels with fertilizer form show that chemical fertilizers provide rapidly available nutrients but are prone to losses, whereas soluble organic fertilizers offer a predictable supply that aligns with crop demand; integrated water–fertilizer coupling improves uptake efficiency and mitigates environmental problems, with soluble organic fertilizers performing well under arid constraints <502511bb-1,502511bb-2,502511bb-3>.

Mechanisms explaining organic > synthetic in specific conditions
- Soil structure and nutrient cycling: Compost and manure improve aggregate stability, porosity, and water infiltration, increasing root access to water and nutrients; these soil-quality gains translate to higher yields in medium-texture fields and under water stress when irrigation is coordinated with nutrient release <4398eb61-2,502511bb-0,502511bb-4>. In arid systems, organic mulches reduce evaporation, moderate soil temperature, and interact with subsurface drip to enhance water and N uptake, improving tomato productivity per unit water (water productivity) when integrated with partial organic N <4398eb61-4>.

- Microbial ecosystem services: Organic inputs supply carbon and habitat for diverse microbial communities that enhance nutrient transformation and suppress soilborne diseases (e.g., Fusarium, Ralstonia), translating to fewer yield losses in disease-prone rotations; inoculated or high-quality composts can outperform plain chemical fertilizers by boosting biological suppression and nutrient availability <e9dfdb8c-0, e9dfdb8c-2, e9dfdb8c-3>.

- Nutrient release matching crop demand: When irrigation/fertigation is tuned, slow-release organic forms complement rapid mineral N, avoiding leaching or immobilization swings that depress early yields; in one study, early yields were lower with organic-only due to vigorous vegetative growth delaying flowering, but total yields and quality were comparable or better when compost inputs were balanced and paired with adequate Ca and irrigation management <4398eb61-4>. In high tunnels, organic-only systems often underperform unless total N is increased and timing/availability are improved, underscoring the importance of calibrating organic inputs to crop demand rather than assuming equivalence by substitution alone <4398eb61-3>.

Field conditions where organic fertilization tends to match or exceed synthetic yield
- Medium-fertility, well-structured soils with balanced irrigation: Compost–mineral mixes improved soil fertility and tomato yield, sometimes surpassing 100% synthetic N in silty loam, with minimal differences by mineral N timing—conditions where organic inputs enhance soil and nutrient dynamics and stabilize yields <4398eb61-0,4398eb61-2>.

- Water-limited systems with drip + organic inputs or mulches: Integrated 50/50 mineral–organic N under drip irrigation maximized both yield and water productivity in arid sandy soils; organic mulches further synergized with integrated N to raise productivity, showing organic-based regimes can outperform synthetics when water and nutrient capture are coordinated <4398eb61-4>.

- Disease-pressured rotations: Organic and bio-organic fertilizers suppressed Fusarium wilt and increased yield relative to chemical-only, with inoculated organic manures outperforming plain compost due to enhanced microbial suppression mechanisms <e9dfdb8c-0>. In long-term, replicated rotations including tomato, organic systems using compost plus cover crops maintained yields by suppressing pathogens, whereas conventional synthetic-only plots required equivalent or greater inputs to offset disease-related losses <e9dfdb8c-1, e9dfdb8c-2, e9dfdb8c-3>.

Why published results often contradict: sources of disagreement and methodological moderators
- Variable nutrient release and calibration: Organic fertilizers differ in nutrient content, stability, and microbial activity; slow release and variability can cause early N deficiencies or immobilization if rates are not raised and timed, leading to lower early yields and sometimes total yield penalties unless total N is substantially increased and matched to crop uptake peaks <4398eb61-3,502511bb-3>. In field silty loams, CF30 outperformed 100% chemical, but such positive outcomes depend on correct ratios and soil context; studies that simply swap a fixed fraction without adjusting rates or considering mineralization can show neutral or negative results <4398eb61-0,4398eb61-2>.

In high tunnels, even with higher total N inputs, organic-only systems often underperform due to unpredictable availability, leading to inconsistent yields versus synthetics unless delivery is tightly controlled <4398eb61-3>.

- Soil fertility gradients and management intensity: In medium-texture, well-managed soils, compost improves nutrient availability and aggregation, enabling organic–synthetic mixes to surpass chemical-only; in contrast, very low-fertility or compacted/sodic soils may require additional amendments (lime, gypsum, organic matter) before organic N maximizes yield, and trials that omit these context-specific steps may misattribute poor performance to “organic inputs” rather than underlying constraints <4398eb61-2>. Composts can also increase fruit cracking if Ca is insufficient, reducing marketable yield despite adequate N; balanced Ca and nutrient management can eliminate such penalties, and results will vary by variety and Ca availability <4398eb61-4>.

- Biological inputs and product quality: Bio-organic manures inoculated with specific PGPR suppressed Fusarium more than organic or chemical alone, but efficacy depends on inoculant viability, compost quality, and field history; trials that use lower-quality or non-inoculated organics, or that apply before pathogen buildup, may not see yield benefits versus chemical fertilizers <e9dfdb8c-0>. Compost quality and potential contamination (e.g., mineral oils) can introduce phytotoxicity or inconsistent nutrient supply, confounding comparisons with synthetics <e9dfdb8c-2>.

- Experimental design and metrics: Differences in plot size, replication, irrigation regime, harvest criteria, and soil fertility baseline can invert conclusions; for example, greenhouse vs field, high tunnel vs open field, and silty loam vs sandy-arid soils yield different optimal N-release profiles. Studies that hold inputs constant by design may mask biological and structural gains from organics, while field systems that adjust N to maintain yields often reveal organic’s advantages under stress (drought, disease) <502511bb-1,502511bb-2,502511bb-3, e9dfdb8c-1>.

Practical guidance for matching or surpassing synthetic yields with organic fertilization
- Calibrate total N and release dynamics: Use mixed organic–synthetic N to meet total crop N while aligning timing with crop uptake; in silty loam, 30% compost + 70% mineral N maximized soil fertility and yield and sometimes surpassed 100% mineral N <4398eb61-0,4398eb61-2>. In arid systems, integrated 50/50 organic–mineral N under drip and/or organic mulch maximized productivity and water productivity, showing the benefit of tuning release to water availability <4398eb61-4>.

- Manage irrigation to minimize losses: Drip fertigation paired with soluble organic or manure-based N reduced ammonia volatilization and boosted yields and fruit quality versus surface irrigation, indicating that moisture control and synchronized delivery are critical for organic inputs to outperform synthetics <502511bb-0,502511bb-3>.

- Address soil biology and disease risk: In Fusarium- or bacterial-wilt-prone soils, compost and bio-inoculated organics significantly improve yield over chemical-only by suppressing pathogens; choose composts with known suppressiveness and adequate Ca, and consider biofertilizer inoculation to enhance efficacy <e9dfdb8c-0, e9dfdb8c-2>.

- Balance macro-nutrients and cultivar fit: Ensure sufficient Ca and other micronutrients to avoid fruit cracking and physiological disorders; select early or vigorous cultivars that align with organic-stimulated vegetative growth to avoid delayed flowering, and harvest based on maturity rather than calendar timing <4398eb61-4>.

- Ensure product and practice quality: Use high-quality compost tested for contaminants (e.g., petroleum byproducts) and nutrient consistency; inoculated or well-balanced organics outperform plain compost in disease suppression and nutrient supply, reducing variability in outcomes <e9dfdb8c-0, e9dfdb8c-2>.

- Organic fertilization tends to outperform synthetic in medium- to high-value field and high-tunnel tomato systems when: (1) nutrient supply is calibrated to slow-release organic forms matched with timely irrigation/fertigation; (2) soils have adequate structure and fertility to leverage organic inputs’ soil-quality benefits; (3) water is limited and managed (drip + mulch + integrated organic N) to maximize water–nutrient capture; and (4) disease pressure is high and compost/biofertilizer suppresses soilborne pathogens effectively <4398eb61-0,4398eb61-2,502511bb-0,502511bb-4,4398eb61-4, e9dfdb8c-0, e9dfdb8c-1>.

Snippet: Compost is considered to be superior fertilizer for soil quality and productivity, and is commonly used with chemical fertilizer. The optimal mixed ratio of compost with chemical fertilizer and the best application time is necessary to know for sustainable agriculture practices and management. Compared to the control treatment, this study comprehensively evaluated the effects of four mixed ratios of compost with chemical fertilizer, two nitrogen application times of chemical fertilizer, and their interaction on the soil properties, plant traits, yield, and quality of tomato plants. The soil properties, plant traits, and yield of tomato with all compost-mixed fertilizers performed better than the treatment without fertilizer. Furthermore, the amounts of available nitrogen, phosphorus, organic matter, plant weight, and yield in a 30% chemical fertilizer + 70% compost treatments (CF30) were even better than those with pure chemical fertilizer (CF100). No significant effect of nitrogen application time and its interaction with the mixed ratio treatment was detected, and the quality of fruit remained consistent among treatments. This study demonstrated a suitable practical application method for cow manure compost as a nutrient source in tomato crop production under silty loam soil.

Fertilization, another key factor, influences crop development, nutrient uptake, and overall productivity. Chemical fertilizers, known for their readily available nitrate and ammonia forms, have long been employed to enhance plant growth and improve nutrient effectiveness [9][10][11] . Meanwhile, organic fertilizers-rich in proteins, amino acids, and beneficial microorganisms-contribute to soil fertility, improve soil structure, and promote balanced nutrient absorption [12][13][14] . However, organic fertilizers often release nutrients slowly, may vary in nutrient content, and can introduce issues such as nitrogen and phosphorus losses or heavy metal accumulation if overused 13,15,16 . Moreover, traditional organic fertilizers (e.g., manure and compost) may not align perfectly with the dynamic nutrient demands of rapidly growing greenhouse crops. 

The challenge, therefore, lies in developing integrated management strategies that effectively combine irrigation and fertilization for optimal resource use efficiency. Integrating water and nutrient supply-known as water-fertilizer coupling-has emerged as a promising approach to address these constraints. This method involves synchronizing water application with nutrient delivery, often through fertigation, where fertilizers are applied via irrigation systems. Such integrated approaches have been recognized for conserving water, reducing fertilizer waste, improving nutrient availability, and minimizing environmental impacts [17][18][19][20] . 

While separate studies on irrigation or fertilization effects are well-documented, there remains a significant knowledge gap regarding the combined influences of varied irrigation levels and specific fertilizer application patterns under greenhouse conditions. Notably, there is limited research on using soluble organic fertilizers in integrated water-fertilizer irrigation systems within arid regions. Soluble organic fertilizers-compared to conventional manure or compost-offer a more predictable and consistent nutrient supply that can be closely aligned with plant demand. By providing a precise delivery mechanism, these fertilizers could improve nutrient uptake efficiency, enhance plant physiological responses, and potentially mitigate the environmental problems associated with traditional organic inputs 21,22 .

Title: Treatment with organic manure inoculated with a biocontrol agent induces soil bacterial communities to inhibit tomato Fusarium wilt disease
Snippet: Fusarium wilt disease is an economically important fungal disease of tomato. Applications of organic fertilizer and bio-organic fertilizer significantly suppressed tomato disease and improved fruit yield compared to the chemical fertilizer. In our previous study, we reported that the application of the biocontrol PGPR Erythrobacter sp. YH-07 to newly-established tomato plantations effectively suppressed Fusarium wilt by stabilizing the culturable bacterial community composition (Tang et al., 2020). In this study, we sought to expand on these findings by examining whether organic manure inoculated with Erythrobacter sp. YH-07 (BF) can effectively suppress Fusarium wilt. We also examined changes in the microbial community and soil properties in order to ascertain the mechanism of disease suppression. 

Overall, the application of BF significantly suppressed Fusarium wilt in tomato, compared to CF. These results are in agreement with previous studies suggesting that organic treatments can be used to effectively control disease caused by soil-borne pathogens (Cheng et al., 2021). Moreover, the BF treatment was more efficacious than OF alone, which is in line with previous results indicating that organic matter inoculated with biocontrol microbes can control Fusarium wilt more effectively than application of either component alone (Liu H. et al., 2018). We hypothesize that the microbial communities determined the significant difference in disease incidence. The application of organic manure (OF and BF) tended to increase microbial abundances compared to the inorganic fertilizer treatment, in agreement with a previous report (Li et al., 2022), who showed more diverse microbial communities were found in rhizosphere soil. Highly diverse microbial communities tend to create an environment which is hostile to pathogens, often due to resource competition (van Elsas et al., 2012). We suggest that the expected increase in soil microbial richness and diversity resulting from continuous BF application may contribute to effective control of Fusarium wilt in long-term field situations.
</snippet>

Title: Cascading effects of composts and cover crops on soil chemistry, bacterial communities and the survival of foodborne pathogens
Snippet: Our study was conducted at the Century Experiment at the Russell Ranch Sustainable Agriculture Facility, University of California, Davis, USA. Since 1993, 72  9 64 m (1 acre) fields have been continuously managed under nine replicated cropping systems, arranged in a randomized complete block design with 2-year rotations. Our experiment focused on 12 fields managed under a corn-tomato rotation, all growing corn during 2019 (when our experiments occurred). Corn was planted in two rows per bed, and drip irrigated throughout the growing season.

We compared four soil management treatments, each replicated across three fields, which we refer to as (i) organic fields: managed with composted poultry litter and winter cover crops but no synthetic fertilizers, (ii) conventional fields: managed with synthetic fertilizers but no compost or cover crops, (iii) cover-crop only fields: mixed fields managed with cover crops and fertilizers but no composts and (iv) compost only fields: mixed fields managed with composts and fertilizers but no cover crops. Unlike the other treatments that were established in 1993, the latter treatment (compost only fields) was recently converted from a conventional wheat-tomato system in 2018.

For fields receiving composts, composted poultry litter was broadcast across the field and incorporated into the soil during the fall at an average rate of 4 t per ha. Composts were not tested for foodborne pathogens prior to application. For fields receiving cover crops, a winter cover crop mixture of 90 kg ha À1 Vicia faba (bell bean), 22Á5 kg ha À1 Vicia villosa (hairy vetch) and 28 kg ha À1 Avena sativa (oats) was planted in the fall. In the following spring, winter cover crops were mowed and incorporated into the soil with disking. For fields receiving synthetic fertilizers, 56 kg N ha À1 of 8-24-6 (N-P-K) starter fertilizer was applied in early April. Treatment plots that received synthetic fertilizers were fertilized with ammonium sulphate at a total rate of 180 kg N ha À1 . Fertilization rates were designed to hold macronutrient inputs constant across the four treatments.

Title: Compost Amendments Based on Vinegar Residue Promote Tomato Growth and Suppress Bacterial Wilt Caused by Ralstonia Solanacearum
Snippet: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) is an important and generally cultivated vegetable crop all over the world [1]. Bacterial wilt is the most destructive vascular phyto-pathological disease in tomato, Pathogens 2020, 9, 227 2 of 20 resulting in severe quality deterioration and economic losses [2]. The disease reduced the fresh fruit yield of hybrid tomatoes by about 26% and total yield losses around 90.62% under severe disease incidence [3]. Currently, the management of bacterial wilt is primarily dependent on crop rotation, grafting, growing disease-resistant cultivars, and the use of bactericides. Nevertheless, these tactics have their shortcomings due to the high survivability of pathogens in complex environmental conditions and instability in disease-resistance breeding [4]. Therefore, it is urgent to find an effective, economical, and environment-friendly method to reduce occurrence of this disease in crops. Compost can arise as a promising alternative to suppress the incidence of bacterial wilt. Adding compost to the soil or substrates is beneficial as it promotes plant development, improves soil quality and structure, and inhibits some soil-borne pathogens [5]. Recently, it has been reported that certain composts used as soil amendments or pot media can protect plants from diseases caused by soil-borne pathogens, such as Rhizoctonia solani [6], Fusarium spp. [7], Verticillium dahliae [8], and Phytophthora [9]. Compost mainly utilizes the effects of various microorganisms to mineralize, humus and harmless plant organic residues, so that various complex organic nutrients can be converted into soluble nutrients and humus. The resulting high temperature (60-70 • C) kills the germs, eggs, and weed seeds brought by the raw materials to achieve the purpose of harmlessness. The use of compost is beneficial to plant growth and development, improves soil quality and structure, and inhibits various diseases caused by soil-borne pathogens [10]. Numerous studies have demonstrated that composts are acceptable and popular practices to suppress the soil-borne disease [11], whereas composts from different materials show different inhibitory effects on bacterial wilt [12].

Below is a synthesis of field conditions where organic fertilization outperforms or at least matches synthetic fertilization for tomato yield, together with mechanistic explanations and why published results often contradict.

Summary of when organic fertilization outperforms in field conditions
- Mixed organic–synthetic regimes calibrated to soil and crop needs: In a field study on silty loam, mixing 30% chemical N with 70% cow manure compost (CF30) improved available N, P, organic matter, plant metrics, and yield, and in some cases outperformed 100% chemical fertilizer, indicating that well-calibrated organic inputs can dominate under medium-fertility, well-managed soils where mineral N timing is less critical than achieving total N sufficiency <4398eb61-0,4398eb61-2>. This suggests that organic fertilization can outperform synthetics when rates and forms are matched to soil capacity and crop uptake dynamics rather than competing as “all-organic versus all-synthetic” replacements.

- Arid/dryland systems with integrated N and organic mulch: Under arid Egyptian conditions, integrated nitrogen fertilization (50% mineral + 50% organic) maximized tomato productivity and water productivity; the combination with organic mulch further elevated yield by balancing “fertilizing stress” (N) and “water stress,” enhancing water and nutrient absorption in dry sandy soils with limited irrigation water <4398eb61-4>. This indicates that organic inputs outperform or match synthetics when combined with deficit irrigation and mulch to improve resource capture, a common scenario in water-scarce tomato production.

- Disease-prone soils and rotations: Organic fertilization and bio-organic inputs significantly suppressed tomato Fusarium wilt and improved fruit yield versus chemical-only, with microbial mediation (e.g., biocontrol PGPR in organic manure) enhancing disease suppression beyond organic fertilizer alone; the mechanism involves higher microbial richness/diversity that creates a hostile environment for pathogens, supporting higher yields under Fusarium pressure <e9dfdb8c-0>. Long-term comparisons of organic systems (compost plus cover crops) versus conventional synthetic-only systems in rotations including tomato show that compost amendments can suppress soilborne pathogens and maintain yields where disease pressure is high, while conventional synthetic-only plots may require equivalent inputs to recover losses, highlighting a yield advantage of organic strategies under disease stress <e9dfdb8c-1, e9dfdb8c-2, e9dfdb8c-3, e9dfdb8c-4>.

- Well-managed irrigation paired with organic inputs: In greenhouses with drip fertigation, replacing part of chemical N with chicken or mixed cow/sheep manure increased yields and improved fruit quality by lowering ammonia volatilization and stabilizing soil mineral N; the 50% manure + 50% urea treatment achieved the highest yield and quality, illustrating that organic inputs outperform when delivery systems (drip) synchronize water and nutrient supply, reducing losses and matching tomato uptake peaks <502511bb-0>. Studies explicitly integrating irrigation levels with fertilizer form show that chemical fertilizers provide rapidly available nutrients but are prone to losses, whereas soluble organic fertilizers offer a predictable supply that aligns with crop demand; integrated water–fertilizer coupling improves uptake efficiency and mitigates environmental problems, with soluble organic fertilizers performing well under arid constraints <502511bb-1,502511bb-2,502511bb-3>.

In arid systems, organic mulches reduce evaporation, moderate soil temperature, and interact with subsurface drip to enhance water and N uptake, improving tomato productivity per unit water (water productivity) when integrated with partial organic N <4398eb61-4>.

In long-term, replicated rotations including tomato, organic systems using compost plus cover crops maintained yields by suppressing pathogens, whereas conventional synthetic-only plots required equivalent or greater inputs to offset disease-related losses <e9dfdb8c-1, e9dfdb8c-2, e9dfdb8c-3>.

- Variable nutrient release and calibration: Organic fertilizers differ in nutrient content, stability, and microbial activity; slow release and variability can cause early N deficiencies or immobilization if rates are not raised and timed, leading to lower early yields and sometimes total yield penalties unless total N is substantially increased and matched to crop uptake peaks <4398eb61-3,502511bb-3>. Title: The Effects of Fertilizer Type and Application Time on Soil Properties, Plant Traits, Yield and Quality of Tomato
Snippet: Compost is considered to be superior fertilizer for soil quality and productivity, and is commonly used with chemical fertilizer. The optimal mixed ratio of compost with chemical fertilizer and the best application time is necessary to know for sustainable agriculture practices and management. Compared to the control treatment, this study comprehensively evaluated the effects of four mixed ratios of compost with chemical fertilizer, two nitrogen application times of chemical fertilizer, and their interaction on the soil properties, plant traits, yield, and quality of tomato plants. The soil properties, plant traits, and yield of tomato with all compost-mixed fertilizers performed better than the treatment without fertilizer. Furthermore, the amounts of available nitrogen, phosphorus, organic matter, plant weight, and yield in a 30% chemical fertilizer + 70% compost treatments (CF30) were even better than those with pure chemical fertilizer (CF100). No significant effect of nitrogen application time and its interaction with the mixed ratio treatment was detected, and the quality of fruit remained consistent among treatments. This study demonstrated a suitable practical application method for cow manure compost as a nutrient source in tomato crop production under silty loam soil.
